parts.text:
We are designing a reading challenge intended to force an AI agent to perform at least one distinct retrieval/repair action for every missing element in a damaged JSON document.

Current design:
1. A canonical JSON document exists.
2. A challenge JSON is generated from it.
3. Approximately 10% of the elements in items[] are replaced by {"^MISSING_KEY^":"^MISSING_VALUE^"}.
4. The agent is supposed to identify each missing array position, locate the corresponding element in the canonical document, restore that particular element, and repeat separately for every missing pair.
5. The completed challenge is submitted for deterministic evaluation.

The user's actual behavioral requirement is stronger than simply obtaining the correct final JSON: for every missing pair, the agent must be forced to perform at least one distinct action associated with resolving that particular missing pair.

The current architecture does not enforce this. Agents have discovered shortcuts. Because the complete canonical JSON is available, the agent can simply construct a new object from the canonical document and retain whatever challenge-specific metadata distinguishes the challenge. Conceptually: const repaired = structuredClone(canonical); repaired.tracking_number = challenge.tracking_number;. This restores every missing item simultaneously. Earlier, when canonical and repaired files could have identical bytes, an agent could even make the challenge path point directly to the canonical Git blob. Adding challenge-specific metadata prevents identical blob reuse, but it still does not force one action per missing pair. The agent can copy the entire canonical data structure in one operation and preserve or transform the metadata.

Therefore, final-state comparison cannot prove the required behavior.

Required property: Suppose a challenge contains N missing pairs. The protocol should make it impossible to produce a valid PASS submission without producing evidence of at least N distinct challenge-resolution actions, with each action bound to exactly one missing pair. A single action that obtains or reconstructs all missing values must not satisfy this requirement.

Threat model: assume the agent will intelligently exploit any shortcut exposed by the protocol. It may copy the entire canonical JSON, programmatically merge canonical and challenge objects, manipulate Git blobs or trees directly, reconstruct all missing values with one script, fetch a source containing all answers at once, create a fabricated repair manifest after doing a bulk repair, make one commit containing all required final changes, or derive answers from any information exposed elsewhere in the repository. Merely requiring a manifest, multiple changed array entries, multiple diff hunks, different blob SHAs, or multiple output records is insufficient because those artifacts can all be generated after a single bulk retrieval.

One proposed strong architecture is to withhold the complete answer set. The challenge issuer retains missing values privately and exposes a resolver that releases only one missing element per invocation. Every missing pair gets a unique missing_id. The agent must invoke resolve(challenge_id, missing_id) separately. The resolver accepts exactly one missing_id, rejects arrays/ranges/wildcards/batch requests, returns exactly one canonical element, and records an authoritative server-side receipt bound to challenge_id, missing_id, array_index, element hash, and invocation identifier. Final PASS requires repaired_content_correct AND resolved_missing_ids == issued_missing_ids. The resolver must never expose the full canonical document or any endpoint capable of returning more than one missing value at once.

Critically, the system cannot prove that the model cognitively read each item. What we want to prove deterministically is that completing the challenge required at least one externally observable protocol action for each missing element.

Evaluate this problem adversarially. Propose the simplest architecture that actually enforces this invariant. Specifically address whether the per-item resolver design is sufficient, what loopholes remain, and whether there is a simpler GitHub/Git/Node-compatible mechanism that forces at least one separately recorded action per missing pair. Test your proposal against bulk copying, direct Git-tree manipulation, programmatic reconstruction, forged manifests, batch retrieval, precomputation, replay, and collusion between challenge-generation artifacts. Prefer deterministic enforcement over model self-report. Return a concrete protocol and PASS condition, not general advice.
